# Technical Marketing in the Age of AI · Article III of Volume I

## 01 · The Condition · What is happening to the GTM stack

Something is moving through enterprise software go-to-market right now. It is not a threat. It is a compression. Every function that produces structured technical content for the sales motion is being operated on by AI tooling that absorbs the mechanical labor of production. Decks get drafted. Competitive summaries get generated. Deployment guides get assembled. The pipeline from raw product knowledge to formatted artifact is collapsing.

The compression is documented. Gartner projected that 40 percent of enterprise applications would be integrated with task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than five percent in 2025.[^1] Salesforce reduced support headcount from nine thousand to approximately five thousand. Marc Benioff stated publicly that the company would hire no new software engineers in fiscal year 2026. Microsoft, Workday, Atlassian, and Oracle each cited AI efficiency as the structural rationale for headcount reduction across adjacent functions.[^2]

The compression is real. The question is what it compresses and what it does not. The answer to that question determines whether technical marketing contracts with the rest of the GTM stack or occupies something different.

> *The compression is real. The question is what it compresses and what it does not.*

## 02 · The Compression Layer · What AI actually absorbs

The work AI compresses is artifact production. The mechanical translation of existing knowledge into structured format. A language model given a product brief and a competitor's published positioning can produce a useful competitive summary in minutes. The same model, given a feature description and a reference architecture, can draft a technical slide. Given a pricing table and a set of published proof points, it can assemble a first-pass evaluation framework.

This is not nothing. Artifact production has consumed a substantial portion of the technical marketing role's time for as long as the role has existed. The TME who spent four hours building a competitive teardown deck now has tooling that produces a draft in forty minutes. The hours freed are real. The compression is net positive for the practitioner who understands how to use it.

What it does not compress is the judgment that decides which artifact to build, which claim to anchor it to, and whether the claim holds under the questioning it will face. A model can draft a competitive teardown. It cannot decide whether to lead with the architectural weakness or the pricing gap, because that decision depends on which competitor the prospect is currently evaluating, what the analyst who will see this deck actually cares about, and what the engineering team will actually stand behind if pushed. Those inputs do not live in a prompt. They live in the room.

The room is where technical marketing lives.

## 03 · The Trust Gap · Why technically capable buyers do not trust what AI produces

The enterprise software buyer most likely to evaluate a complex product is also the buyer most likely to distrust AI-generated content about it. This is not sentiment. It is data.

Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey found that trust in AI accuracy fell eleven percentage points in a single year, from forty percent to twenty-nine.[^3] When asked what they would still want from a human even if AI could do most coding tasks, seventy-five percent of developers said they would not trust AI answers. The number-one frustration, cited by forty-five percent of respondents, was dealing with AI solutions that were almost right but not quite.

Almost right is the precise failure mode that kills a technical sale. A principal engineer reviewing an architecture diagram that is almost right does not engage with the content. They disengage from the company. A CISO reviewing a security questionnaire that overpromises by one degree does not note the caveat. They flag the vendor. The tolerance for almost right in the rooms where technical marketing works is zero.

McKinsey's 2026 AI Trust Maturity Survey found that seventy-four percent of organizations identify inaccuracy as a highly relevant AI risk, and nearly two-thirds cite security and risk concerns as the top barrier to scaling agentic AI deployment.[^4] The CEO of Stack Overflow, speaking to McKinsey's technology practice, put the condition plainly: "Having high-quality, expert-verified knowledge inside organizations has become critical, not a nice-to-have."[^5]

Expert-verified knowledge is a job description. It is the technical marketer's job description.

> *Almost right is the precise failure mode that kills a technical sale.*

## 04 · The Favorable Position · Where technical marketing sits on the compression map

Article I of this volume introduced the function matrix: technical depth on one axis, commercial orientation on the other.[^6] The matrix identifies the disciplines that touch enterprise software GTM, and it places technical marketing alone in the quadrant that requires high scores on both. That position is relevant here for a different reason.

When AI compresses artifact production across the GTM stack, the disciplines most exposed are those that produce structured content as their primary output. Technical writing. First-pass documentation. Boilerplate competitive summaries. Standard sales decks. Those outputs were already mechanical. AI has now made them more efficiently mechanical. The practitioners who built their value on producing those outputs at volume are facing genuine compression.

The disciplines least exposed are those where the output is judgment under commercial pressure rather than structured content at volume. The disciplines where the question is not how to produce the artifact but which artifact to produce, which claim to stake, and whether the company can defend it when the analyst pushes back. That question requires holding the buyer's specific evaluation context, the company's commercial pressure, the engineering team's honest constraints, and the competitive landscape simultaneously. It cannot be usefully delegated to a model that has none of those inputs.

The compression does not threaten the favorable quadrant. It reveals it. When AI absorbs the production work that surrounded the judgment, the judgment becomes visible as the scarce resource. What was always the most valuable thing the role did becomes the explicit center of it.

## 05 · The Clarification · What the discipline becomes when the production layer lifts

The compression of artifact production does not remove work from the technical marketing role. It removes the part of the work that was never the role's highest-leverage contribution. The hours that went into first drafts, formatting, initial research compilation, and basic content assembly get absorbed by tooling. The hours that remain are the ones that determined whether the first draft was worth producing in the first place.

Which competitor to address. Which architectural claim is defensible and which overpromises by a degree the engineering team will not stand behind in a live briefing. Whether the demo should show the integration or the native capability, and why that choice changes depending on whether the audience is a Gartner analyst or a buying committee's principal engineer. That decision set has always been the role's real work. AI does not touch it.

> *The more AI produces, the more essential the verification layer becomes.*

## 06 · The Practitioner's Posture · What this requires in practice

The technical marketer who understands this transition does not resist AI tooling. They use it to accelerate the production layer while protecting their editorial authority over what the production layer produces. The draft that used to take four hours now takes forty minutes. The judgment about whether the draft is accurate, whether the claim holds, whether the framing serves the buyer's actual evaluation question: that judgment takes exactly as long as it always did, because it requires the same inputs it always required.

The transition asks two things of the practitioner. First, enough comfort with AI tooling to use it without deferring to it. The practitioner who defers to the model's framing rather than evaluating it against the product's actual engineering reality is producing AI-assisted content that will fail under buyer pressure. The model's framing is a starting point. The practitioner's judgment is the edit. Second, clarity about which work to protect. The editorial decisions, which claim, which competitor, which audience framing, are not candidates for delegation. The verification pass on every artifact that enters the sales motion is not optional. The accountability is not transferable.

The discipline does not shrink when AI gets better. It becomes more important. When every competitor's field team is producing AI-generated technical content at the same volume, the differentiator is the technical marketer who can verify what that content actually claims, hold the company's honest engineering reality in the same hand, and decide what to put in front of the analyst on Tuesday. That practitioner is not being replaced by the tooling. They are being revealed by it.

## 07 · The Position · The structural argument, stated plainly

AI compresses the production of structured technical content across every GTM function. Sales engineering, product marketing, technical writing, developer advocacy: all of them are producing artifacts more efficiently than they were eighteen months ago. The mechanical labor of assembly is cheaper everywhere.

What does not get cheaper is the judgment that decides which artifact to produce, which claim to anchor it to, and whether the company can defend that claim in the room where the buyer decides. That judgment is the definition of technical marketing. It has always been the definition of technical marketing. The production work that surrounded it was necessary to execute the judgment. It was never the judgment itself.

The compression removes the surrounding work. What remains is the discipline's core. The discipline does not contract under AI compression. It clarifies. And what it clarifies is what it always was: editorial authority over technical evidence, applied one decision at a time, under buyer pressure, where the call matters.

> *The discipline does not contract under AI compression. It clarifies.*

# Glossary of Technical Marketing · Working Reference

> A working reference for the terms practitioners use. Definitions as the field applies them across enterprise software, AI, infrastructure, and hardware. Not as a dictionary would.

## Scope

This glossary covers the operational vocabulary of technical marketing as practiced across enterprise software, AI, infrastructure, and hardware. Definitions prioritize field usage over etymological correctness. Where a term is used differently across companies or contexts, the definition reflects the most common practitioner interpretation.

---

**Agentic AI** · AI systems that plan and execute multi-step tasks autonomously, using tools, APIs, and external data sources, rather than responding to a single prompt and stopping. The distinction from generative AI is operational rather than architectural. A generative model answers a question. An agentic system pursues a goal through a sequence of actions, evaluating intermediate results and adjusting. For technical marketing, agentic AI is both a product category to market and a production accelerator.

**Analyst briefing** · A structured presentation delivered to a technology research analyst at Gartner, Forrester, IDC, or a comparable firm, with the goal of accurately positioning a company's product within the analyst's ongoing research and evaluation frameworks. An analyst briefing is not a sales call. A single briefing can influence how an entire market segment perceives a product category for twelve to eighteen months. Technical marketing owns the substance of analyst briefings.

**AR cycle** (analyst relations cycle) · The structured, recurring process by which a company engages with technology research analysts: briefing them on product direction, responding to research inquiries, participating in evaluation frameworks, and tracking resulting position changes in published reports. The AR cycle is typically annual. Technical marketing owns the substance of AR cycle participation. Analyst position shift in the next AR cycle is one of the clearest measurable outcomes the role produces.

**Architecture overview** · A structured diagram and accompanying explanation that describes how a software product is built, how its components relate to each other, and how it connects to the systems a buyer already operates. An architecture overview is one of the most durable artifacts in the technical marketing portfolio. It serves buyers at the evaluation stage who need to understand not just what the product does but how it does it.

**Battlecard** · A concise, structured reference document that equips a sales or pre-sales team member to handle a specific competitor in a live deal. A decision aid, not a research document. Length discipline is required: a battlecard that requires twenty minutes to read before a call is not a battlecard. It is a white paper with a competitive posture.

**Benchmark artifact** · A structured technical deliverable, including performance data, comparative specifications, and reference designs, that proves a product's claim against a measurable standard. The primary demo archetype of hardware and semiconductor companies, where the audience is a procurement engineer, a standards body, or a technical architect evaluating performance under defined conditions. The SE does not demo it. The buyer's engineers interrogate it. Source: /the-technical-marketer, /glossary.

**Buying committee** · The group of stakeholders within a prospect organization who collectively influence or make a purchase decision, typically spanning technical evaluators, business sponsors, economic buyers, procurement, legal, and security functions. No single demo, no single artifact, and no single conversation wins a buying committee. Technical marketing builds for the entire committee.

**Calibration band** · The range of technical depth at which marketing content is most effective in a complex enterprise sale: enough depth to give a technically capable buyer a surface to evaluate, but not so much that the content becomes an enablement exercise rather than a persuasion instrument. Technical marketing occupies the band deliberately. Source: /what-is-technical-marketing, /glossary.

**Champion** · An individual within a buying organization who actively advocates for a vendor's product internally, carries the evaluation forward when the vendor is not in the room, and is willing to stake personal credibility on the purchase recommendation. The materials technical marketing produces are the tools a champion uses to do their internal selling.

**Competitive engagement** · An active sales situation in which the buyer is simultaneously evaluating one or more named competitors. In a competitive engagement, the demo, the technical narrative, and the battlecard all change character under competitive pressure. Win rate on contested deals is one of the clearest direct measures of whether technical marketing's competitive work is landing.

**Configured environment** · A live software tenant built to prove that the platform does what the positioning claims, using realistic data, configured workflows, and the personas a buyer recognizes as their own. The primary demo archetype of platform companies (ServiceNow, Salesforce, Workday). The technical marketer owns the architecture, the data integrity, and the scenario coherence. The sales engineer deploys it in the field. Source: /the-technical-marketer, /glossary.

**Demo** · A structured, live or recorded presentation of software in operation, designed to produce a specific belief in a specific audience at a specific stage of a sale or evaluation. The unit of a demo is not the feature. It is the belief the feature is meant to produce. A practitioner who cannot state the target belief before building the demo is building a tour.

**Demo coherence** · The degree to which every element of a demo, including data, workflow, persona, and narrative, serves a single, consistent argument rather than demonstrating coverage of features. Demo coherence is the primary quality signal for technical marketing output.

**Discovery call** · A structured conversation between a vendor's sales or pre-sales team and a prospect, conducted early in the sales cycle to understand the buyer's current environment, the problem they are trying to solve, and the criteria they will use to evaluate solutions. Technical marketing builds the frameworks that make discovery consistent; it does not typically conduct discovery calls.

**Economic buyer** · The individual within a buying organization who holds final budget authority. The economic buyer is often not the person running the evaluation. Technical marketing's relationship to the economic buyer is indirect: the function rarely presents to them directly, but the materials it produces are what the champion uses to make the case in meetings the vendor cannot attend.

**Editorial judgment** · The practitioner's capacity to decide, under commercial pressure, which technical evidence to present to which audience, in what order, with what framing, and at what level of depth, such that the result advances a specific buyer's evaluation. The defining skill of technical marketing and the dimension most resistant to compression by AI tooling.

**Evaluation conversion** · The rate at which opportunities entering a formal technical evaluation stage result in a technical win. The most direct signal that technical marketing content is working at the stage where it matters. Impressions, clicks, and form fills measure awareness. Evaluation conversion measures whether the discipline's output is actually winning evaluations.

**Field activation** · The percentage of the sales and pre-sales field team actively using the current validated demo, competitive battlecards, and current technical positioning in live customer conversations. Low field activation is diagnostic: it can indicate content that does not fit how SCs are actually selling, a communication failure, or content that is technically accurate but not usable in the time constraints of a real customer conversation.

**Integration guide** · A structured technical document that explains how to connect a vendor's product to a buyer's existing systems, covering authentication, data flow, configuration requirements, and common failure modes, written at the depth required for a technical evaluator to assess integration feasibility during a purchase evaluation.

**Interactive proof** · A trial environment or sandbox that a buyer runs themselves, converting skepticism through direct experience rather than through a vendor-led demonstration. The primary demo archetype of PLG companies (Datadog, Linear, Vercel). The technical marketer builds both the environment and the narrative layer that makes the experience legible. Source: /the-technical-marketer, /glossary.

**Magic Quadrant** · Gartner's primary market evaluation framework, positioning vendors in one of four quadrants: Leaders, Challengers, Visionaries, or Niche Players. A Magic Quadrant position is one of the most consequential outputs of an AR cycle for an enterprise software company. Technical marketing's contribution to Magic Quadrant position is direct: the briefing materials, demo content, and technical proof points the function produces are what Gartner analysts evaluate when assessing Ability to Execute.

**Pipeline** · The set of active sales opportunities tracked by a revenue organization, representing the total potential closed revenue at any given point. Technical marketing influences pipeline indirectly: by improving evaluation conversion, reducing time-to-decision, and improving win rate on competitive deals, it makes the existing pipeline worth more.

**Playbook** · A structured collection of resources, guidance, and pre-built materials that enables a sales or pre-sales team to execute a defined sales motion consistently across opportunities. The playbook is the distribution mechanism for technical marketing's output.

**Presales** · The organizational function that supports a complex sale from initial prospect engagement through contract signature. Presales is the parent category that contains the sales engineering and solutions consulting functions. Technical marketing is adjacent to presales but distinct: presales runs the play; technical marketing writes the playbook.

**Proof of concept** (POC) · A structured technical evaluation in which the vendor configures and tests their product against a customer's specific environment, data, or use case. A POC that surfaces a genuine product gap is a product signal, not only a deal post-mortem event. Technical marketing is involved in POC strategy: defining the success criteria, the scope, the data requirements, and the evaluation framework before the POC begins. An undefined POC is not a POC. It is a free consulting engagement.

**Proof of value** (POV) · A structured evaluation in which the buyer tests whether a product produces a measurable improvement against a business outcome they have committed to achieving. A POV without a stated value hypothesis is an extended trial with a subjective exit.

**Reference architecture** · A structured technical artifact, typically code, pipelines, notebooks, or integration patterns, that proves a product's claim at the level a technically capable evaluator can interrogate directly. The primary demo archetype of infrastructure and data companies (Databricks, Elastic, CrowdStrike, HashiCorp). The buyer's own engineering team validates it. Closer to a GitHub repo than a slide deck. Source: /the-technical-marketer, /glossary.

**Reference environment** · The canonical configuration of a software product that serves as the authoritative source from which demonstrations, technical content, and evaluation materials are produced. A reference environment is not a demo. It is the infrastructure from which demos are produced. A reference environment without clear ownership is not a reference environment. It is a shared demo instance, and shared demo instances degrade toward incoherence.

**Regis McKenna** · A Silicon Valley marketing strategist who joined National Semiconductor in 1967 and later founded Regis McKenna Inc., becoming one of the earliest practitioners and theorists of technical marketing in the semiconductor and computing industries. In the history of the discipline, McKenna represents the Era I anchor: the point at which technical marketing became a recognized in-house function at product companies.

**RFP** (request for proposal) · A formal procurement document issued by a buying organization that requires vendors to respond to a structured set of questions covering product capabilities, technical architecture, security posture, pricing, implementation approach, and company stability. An RFP response is one of the highest-effort, highest-stakes artifacts in the technical marketing portfolio. Technical marketing's work before the RFP arrives shapes the RFP itself.

**Sales engineer / Solutions consultant** · A technical practitioner embedded in the sales motion whose job is to win individual deals by conducting discovery, running demonstrations, building proofs of concept, and handling technical objections. The SE executes in the field; the technical marketer architects the conditions for that execution.

**Teardown** · A structured competitive analysis of a rival product, conducted by the technical marketing team to understand how the competitor's product actually works, what it can and cannot do, and where it is vulnerable to displacement.

**Technical champion** · A technically credible individual within the buying organization who validates the product's claims to peers and to leadership. Not all champions are technical champions, but in complex enterprise software sales the strongest champions are both.

**Technical marketer** · A senior practitioner of technical marketing, typically with eight or more years in technical product roles, holding editorial authority on what evidence the company presents to its most skeptical audiences. Source: /the-technical-marketer.

**Technical narrative** · The structured, evidence-anchored story the company tells about how its product works and why that matters to a specific audience at a specific stage of an evaluation.

**Technical win** · The formal outcome of a technical evaluation in which the buying committee's technical evaluators conclude that the vendor's product meets their technical requirements and recommend it for commercial consideration. Technical marketing exists to improve technical win rate.

**Time to decision** · The elapsed time between a formal evaluation beginning and a technical win or loss. Technical marketing reduces time to decision by ensuring that the evidence a buyer needs is pre-built, accessible, and calibrated for the relevant evaluation stage.

**Trust layer** · The body of technical marketing content that occupies the calibration band: evidence that is deep enough for a technically capable buyer to trust, but not so deep that it becomes enablement content rather than evaluation content. Source: /what-is-technical-marketing.

---

# Technical Marketing Landscape · The Discipline in Practice

> How enterprise software, AI, and hardware companies staff, title, and place the technical marketing function. Verified from public job postings and named-practitioner accounts. Updated each volume.

The technical marketing function appears in job postings at companies across every category of enterprise software, AI, infrastructure, and hardware. The titles are inconsistent. The org placement varies. The work is recognizably similar.

## Company entries

| Company | Title used | Org placement | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anthropic | Senior Product Marketing Manager | Marketing | Supports the B2B sales motion for Claude for Work. Owns value proposition to enterprise buyers. Distills complex technical and market issues into sales materials across a wide spectrum of AI knowledge. Embeds directly with the sales team. Requires strong storytelling, enterprise sales enablement experience, and deep AI/ML fluency. |
| Autodesk | Technical Marketing Manager | Marketing | Reports into Product Marketing under the CMO organization. Specific to the Autodesk Tandem (Digital Twin) product team. Participates in alpha and beta programs, builds demos and talk tracks. AECO industry focus. |
| AWS | Sr. Technical Product Marketing Manager | Marketing | Inside AWS Product Marketing. Partners with product and GTM teams on portfolio-level strategy and positioning. Container services, serverless, and AI/ML focus areas active. |
| Cisco | Director, Technical Marketing | Presales / Field | Senior IC collaborating across engineering, product management, sales, and the broader industry ecosystem. Data Center Networking Business unit. 15 years networking experience expected. |
| Cohere | Product Marketing Manager | Marketing | Enterprise-facing AI platform. Positions as security-first AI for regulated industries including finance, healthcare, and the public sector. Role requires distilling complex model capabilities into enterprise-grade proof points for technically sophisticated buyers. Sovereign AI positioning. |
| CrowdStrike | Sr. Technical Marketing Manager / Director, Technical Marketing | Marketing | Function named "Product & Technical Marketing" at the VP level. Multiple Directors across product areas: Next-Gen SIEM, Cloud Security, SaaS Security. One of the most explicitly structured technical marketing functions in enterprise cybersecurity. |
| Databricks | Sr. Technical Marketing Engineer | Marketing | Reports to Director of Technical Marketing. Works closely with Lakebase and Databricks Apps teams. Builds demo applications and reference architectures. Primary audience: application developers and data engineers. |
| Datadog | Sr. Technical Product Marketing Manager | Marketing | First hire on the security product marketing team. Owns technical positioning and go-to-market for security offerings. |
| Elastic | Technical Marketing Engineer / Principal Product Marketing Engineer | Marketing | Uses both titles for the same function. Security TME focus includes attack scenario development. Engineer-heritage title convention. |
| IBM (formerly HashiCorp) | Sr. Technical Product Marketing Manager | Marketing | HashiCorp had a named Senior Director of Technical Product Marketing before its 2024 IBM acquisition. Function persists under IBM. Infrastructure software reference archetype. |
| Intel Corporation | Technical Marketing Engineer | Marketing | Processor and platform strategy. Long-established hardware TME function predating the enterprise software version by decades. |
| JFrog | Technical Marketing Manager | Marketing | DevOps and software supply chain security. |

Represents NVIDIA in JEDEC standards bodies. Requires 12 years of memory architecture experience. Hardware TMM predates the enterprise software version by at least two decades. |
| OpenAI | Senior Product Marketing Manager, Platform | Marketing | Covers the API platform business targeting developers, startups, and enterprise. Job description explicitly lists "product marketing, technical marketing, sales engineering" as the qualifying experience track. Partners with Product, Sales, and Comms on positioning, adoption, and competitive differentiation. |
| Oracle | Sr. Principal Technical Product Marketing Manager | Product / Marketing | Owns technical positioning for Oracle Autonomous AI Lakehouse. "Intersection of deep engineering knowledge and strategic marketing." Explicitly leads analyst briefings for Gartner MQ and Forrester Wave. |
| Palo Alto Networks | Principal Technical Marketing Engineer / Director, Technical Marketing Engineering | Marketing | Uses "Technical Marketing Engineering" as the primary title frame. Multiple Directors across Prisma SASE, CDSS, and Cortex. Sits inside Product Marketing. |
| Pure Storage | Sr. Technical Marketing Engineer | Marketing | AI and Portworx (Kubernetes storage) focus. TME title at scale, not TMM. Engineering-heritage naming convention. |
| Red Hat | Technical Marketing Manager | Marketing | Most widely cited public description of the role's day-to-day responsibilities. Role creates technical content, supports developer relations, and executes campaigns aimed at technical audiences. |
| Salesforce (MuleSoft) | Sr. Technical Product Marketing Manager / Technical Product Marketing Director | Marketing | MuleSoft operates as a distinct business unit within Salesforce with its own product marketing org. Sr. TPMM owns demo-building, technical content, and event activations; requires prior background in solutions engineering or product management. Director-level IC owns MuleSoft's flagship portfolio narrative; explicitly seeks practitioners with background as developer, solutions architect, SE, or PM converted to marketing. |
| Salesforce (Slack) | Technical Product Marketing Manager | Marketing | Slack operates as a distinct business unit within Salesforce with its own CMO (Ryan Gavin) and independent marketing org. Role focuses on product positioning, demo strategy for major events, and high-visibility asset creation. Named practitioner (Lauren S.A. Nielsen) transitioned directly from Senior Solutions Engineer. Closest to PLG archetype of any Salesforce-family entry. |
| ServiceNow (incl. Moveworks, acq. Dec 2025) | Sr. Director, Technical Marketing | Marketing | Reports to VP of Technical and Platform Marketing, who reports to VP of Product and Solutions, then CMO. Platform company archetype: TMM inside marketing with direct product partnership. ServiceNow completed the acquisition of Moveworks in December 2025 for $2.85 billion; the technical marketing function now spans both the core Now Platform and the Moveworks product line. |
| Workday | Sr. Technical Product Marketing Manager | Product / Marketing | Sits at the intersection of product, engineering, and GTM for the Workday Build & Platform team. Measures success through platform adoption, analyst engagement, and field readiness. |

## What the table shows

Three org placement archetypes appear consistently. The majority sit inside Marketing and report through a CMO organization. A second group sits at the explicit intersection of product and marketing, with language like "intersection of product, engineering, and field." A smaller number sit closer to the field and presales technical organization.

The title is not standardized. "Technical Marketing Manager," "Technical Product Marketing Manager," and "Technical Marketing Engineer" all appear across companies doing recognizably similar work. Companies with engineering-first cultures use "engineer." Companies with strong marketing org traditions use "manager." The work is the same.

Hardware and semiconductor companies (Intel, NVIDIA) have used these titles formally since the 1960s. The enterprise software version came decades later. AI companies (Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere) are now building the same function for a new product category. The function's roots in hardware are not incidental. They are the origin point. The history is documented in Before the Name.

---

# About Technical Marketing


technicalmarketing.org is a publication for the people who do this work. The technical marketers operating without a shared reference. The practitioners coming into the field who deserve to find something better than scattered job descriptions and vendor blog posts. The senior people whose hard-won judgment has never been collected anywhere visible.


The project is to give a fragmented field a working reference and a record it can collectively own. [The foundational reference page](/what-is-technical-marketing) is the editorial anchor: what the discipline is, where it sits, how it is distinguished from adjacent roles, and why it is structurally positioned to do well in the AI transition. The publication also produces original long-form articles, beginning with [The Technical Marketer](/the-technical-marketer), Article I of Volume 01. The quarterly index curates current thinking from across the field, with editorial commentary that names what each piece gets right and where the conversation needs to go next.


The work is slow on purpose. Defining a discipline that has historically resisted definition takes multiple volumes, multiple contributors, and multiple revisions of foundational pages. The empty spaces in this publication are intentional. They mark the conversations the field still needs to have.


## Who this serves


Five audiences, named directly. Working practitioners who have done this job at scale and want the discipline they have built to be recognizable to the people they work with. Practitioners coming into the role today, including the next generation entering a field that is about to be transformed by AI, who deserve a working definition they can build on rather than invent alone. Senior practitioners and adjacent leaders whose hard-won judgment has not been collected anywhere visible yet. AI GTM practitioners who are building the technical proof layer for foundation models, agent platforms, and AI infrastructure, and who are discovering that the discipline's evaluation-stage tools apply directly to their work even when the product category is new. Hardware and semiconductor technical marketers, for whom the benchmark artifact and reference architecture have been standard practice for decades, and whose history is the origin point the enterprise software version of the role grew from.


## Editorial connection


The publication is edited by Chad Corriveau, founder of [ThinkRoot](https://thinkroot.io), an independent technical marketing advisory practice. The Demo Coherence Index, the Root Cause Field Notes, and other ThinkRoot work appear in the index alongside curated pieces from other practitioners. Every entry is held to the same editorial standard: the strength of the argument and the specificity of the perspective. Inclusion reflects editorial judgment, not commercial consideration. This connection is disclosed deliberately so the editorial decisions can speak for themselves.


## Editorial principles


The publication is curated, not comprehensive. Pieces are included based on the strength of their argument and the specificity of their perspective, not the size of the brand or the popularity of the author. Editorial notes accompany every entry to identify what each piece gets right, where it falls short, and how it fits in the broader conversation. The publication will represent more voices over time, including ones the editor disagrees with, when those voices sharpen the discipline's working definition.


## Submissions and contributions


The publication is actively building its contributor pipeline. Senior practitioners working in technical marketing or adjacent disciplines who want to contribute a piece to a future volume should review the [submissions page](/suggest) for current editorial priorities. Original pieces, recommendations of overlooked work, and respectful disagreement with anything published here are all welcome.


## Publication schedule


New volumes publish quarterly. Volume 01 was published in Spring 2026. Volume 02 publishes in Q3 2026. The foundational reference page is updated continuously as the discipline's working definition sharpens.


---

# Submissions · Suggest a Piece for the Next Volume


Volume 02 publishes in Q3 2026. Submissions, recommendations, and respectful disagreement are welcome from practitioners, editors, and readers who have found something worth including in the next index.


Pieces are evaluated on the strength of the argument and the specificity of the perspective, not the size of the brand or the popularity of the author. Editorial notes accompany every entry, including notes that disagree with what the piece argues.


## Particularly seeking

- Practitioner essays from senior technical marketers, technical product marketers, and solutions marketing leaders inside the major enterprise software categories: hyperscaler and cloud infrastructure, data and analytics platforms, cybersecurity, DevOps and developer tools, AI and ML platforms, workflow and platform software, and observability
- Sharp framework or methodology pieces that go beyond surface-level definitions of the discipline
- Named-author analysis of where the field is shifting under AI pressure
- Historical perspective on how the technical marketing function has evolved across the major enterprise software eras
- Counter-arguments to currently popular framings of the discipline


Especially interested in submissions from practitioners at AWS, Snowflake, ServiceNow, Salesforce, Palo Alto Networks, GitHub, Anthropic, Cloudflare, Datadog, Confluent, MongoDB, HashiCorp, Atlassian, and their peers across these categories.


## What gets declined


Vendor content marketing pieces, generic listicles, AI-generated explainers, and pieces that primarily exist to drive traffic to a commercial offer. The index is curated, not comprehensive. Every entry needs to earn its place by saying something true that isn't being said elsewhere.


## Submit a piece


A URL to the published piece, the author's site, or a draft for proposed original work.


Responses within two weeks.
